So the incentive is for producers to make products out of the least costly, most effective materials, including packaging, which is also often the hardest to recover. Consumers will pay very little more for a "green" product or package.
Later, the product and package is "thrown away" but it never goes really "away". Low income residents, who probably purchase less "stuff" pay the same rate per pound for disposal as the more well-off (who generate more stuff), so the per-pound cost is regressive. 
Recycling is not "free", it is a cost to the County minus the recovery value, which fluctuates. 
None of these costs are in the initial purchase price. We pay them later and disconnected from the initial cost. This is an inefficient supply and demand system

Electric motors usually generate much more torque at 0 speed than an ICE which requires high rpms to produce sufficient power to overcome its own piston compression requirements (remember each piston is only producing power about 25% of the time, and that power stroke needs to power the remaining compression, injection and exhaust strokes) ergo an ICE engine tends to hit its peak torque towards its mid level revs and then needs a gearbox to convert those ~3000rpms into  1 rpm at the wheel. (Diesels tend to have a torque curve that continues to rise with rpms)  Whereas an electric motor generates instant torque at starting thus no need to reduce rpms to wheels, and the rotating magnetic field eventually brakes the amount of current into the stator magnets thus reducing the torque once the rotor is turning. But ultimately the stall torque load of most electric motors is still higher than peak torque in an ICE.
